title: κ, γ, χ and λ before e and i

steps.text: Before an e or i sound (ε, αι, η, ι, υ, ει, οι) Greek moves κ, γ and χ forward, from the back of the mouth to the hard roof behind the gum ridge: κ comes out almost as a k with a y in it, γ is the y of “yes”, χ is the h of “huge” said with a hiss. English does only a little of this, and a reader keeps each letter as it sounds before α or ο. λ goes the same way where an unstressed ι runs on into the next vowel, as in ἥλιος: there λι is one sound, like the lli of “million”.

Say “cool”, then “key”, and feel where your tongue touches: further forward for “key”. Greek κ before e and i sits there, and a little further forward still: καί is close to “kyeh”, with no separate y. Then say “yes” and “huge”: those are γ and χ before e and i. For λ, say “million” and hear the lli as one sound.

Listen to κ in καί and ἐκεῖνος, γ in λέγει and χ in ἔχει: each before an e or i sound, each forward in the mouth. In ἥλιος and χίλια hear λι run on into the vowel after it. Lampas writes that ι as a syllable of its own, as it is said slowly, and that is never wrong.
Each pair has the same letter before a back vowel and before a front one. Hear it move forward: κ in κόπος and κῆπος, γ in γάμον and γέμον, χ in χώραν and χήραν, and in ἔχω and ἔχει.
Say each word after the voice. Before e and i, let the tongue slide forward for κ, γ and χ; in ἥλιος, say λι as one sound, the lli of “million”.
Each κ, γ and χ before an e or i sound is marked: nine of them, four in καί alone. Hear it, then say it, with the tongue forward for every one.
